analysis.one_liner: Creates a national Do Not Track system and gives people rights over the data companies collect about them online.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and a consumer protection subcommittee in October 2021 and never advanced further; it received no vote before Congress adjourned in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The REPAIR Act would have required companies to get your clear, affirmative permission before collecting or selling your personal data, and to let you see, correct, or delete it. It would have created a downloadable "Do Not Track" program, run by the Federal Trade Commission, that tells websites and ad trackers not to harvest your data or serve you targeted advertising. Companies that violated it would face civil penalties, and state attorneys general could sue on residents' behalf. The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users would gain enforceable rights over their personal data: consent before collection, access, correction, deletion, and a one-click national opt-out of data harvesting and targeted advertising, with FTC and state enforcement and civil penalties behind it. Small businesses under $50 million in revenue are exempted, so compliance costs fall on large platforms, data brokers, and ad-tech firms rather than small firms.

how_it_helps.text: Requires companies to get affirmative, express consent before collecting, processing, or transferring a person's data, with consent obtainable or withdrawable through an FTC-designed process.

Creates a national Do Not Track system: a downloadable FTC program that sends a signal to websites, which would then be barred from collecting data for targeted advertising or transferring it to third parties without consent, and barred from penalizing users who send the signal.
Grants individuals rights to see and receive their data, correct inaccurate data, and have data deleted or masked, with those requests extending to third parties that received the data.

Allows FTC enforcement with civil penalties of up to $1,000 per affected person per day for willful violations, plus enforcement by state attorneys general, tribes, and territories, and preserves stronger state privacy laws.
Requires real-time notification of data collection on websites and apps, so people know when they are being tracked and by whom.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that profit from collecting, processing, and selling personal data — especially large internet platforms, data brokers, and ad-tech businesses — would bear compliance costs, lose access to data they currently monetize, and face FTC and state-level penalties.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for companies that collect or sell data would be substantial, and critics of privacy mandates argue these costs can be passed to consumers or used by large incumbents as an advantage over mid-sized firms (though the bill exempts businesses under $50 million in revenue, 500 employees, and 1 million consumers per year).

The bill relies heavily on FTC rulemaking to define the consent process and permissible data uses, so its real-world strength would depend on how the agency writes and enforces the rules rather than on the statute alone.
Requiring pop-up notices and affirmative consent dialogs could add friction to everyday browsing, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the benefit side, the bill would give ordinary internet users legal control over their own data: affirmative consent before collection, rights to delete and correct, a one-click Do Not Track tool with real penalties behind it, and state attorneys general empowered to sue on consumers' behalf. The main honest objections are cost and design: compliance spending by large firms could be passed to consumers or shield smaller competitors (though small businesses are exempted), notification and consent requirements could add friction to everyday browsing, and enforcement would lean heavily on the FTC and state AGs getting it right through rulemaking. Drawbacks are modest relative to what consumers would gain, but the debate the bill might have prompted never occurred.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to a House committee and a subcommittee on arrival and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 30, 2021 by Rep. Bill Posey with three cosponsors and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day.
On October 1, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, where it sat with no further action.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred; the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and large internet platforms, which keep collecting and selling personal data without the consent, deletion, or Do Not Track requirements the bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and large internet platforms

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, but the bill drew no recorded floor support or opposition because it never advanced past referral; no votes were ever taken.

industries.note: Their core business — harvesting personal data and selling it for targeted advertising — would require consent, face minimization limits, and be shut off by the Do Not Track signal. They lose revenue with no offsetting benefit in the bill.

industries.industry: Large internet platforms (social networks, search engines, video sharing)
industries.note: They would face affirmative consent, transparency, deletion, and security requirements, and would have to honor the Do Not Track signal, cutting into ad-targeting revenue. Some benefit from the small business exemption's carve-out, but the big platforms lose.

Targeted advertising, which funds much free online content, would be restricted for users who opt out; the bill allows contextual ads instead. Readers would keep access, but publishers' ad revenue could fall.
Businesses under $50 million in revenue, 500 employees, and 1 million consumers processed are exempt from most requirements, sparing them compliance costs their larger competitors would bear.
